claims.text: The starting Al-Cr-Fe-Ni protective coating has a multilayer architecture with relatively thick individual layers.
The starting coating contains both FCC and BCC phases.
Reducing individual layer thickness increases the density of interfaces in the multilayer coating.
Layer interfaces act as barriers to dislocation glide.
Obstruction of dislocation glide suppresses progressive plastic deformation during sustained loading.
Increasing interfacial density by reducing layer thickness improves the coating's creep resistance.
Thinner-layer coatings will have a lower nanoindentation creep rate than the thicker-layer baseline.
Thinner-layer coatings will resist plastic deformation better than the thicker-layer baseline.
Thinner-layer coatings will exhibit a delayed onset of primary creep relative to the thicker-layer baseline.
Thinner-layer coatings will show improved yield strength over time relative to the thicker-layer baseline.
The interfacial-barrier mechanism is expected to operate under sustained stresses typical of nanoindentation creep testing and at moderate service temperatures.
At extreme temperatures or very high stresses, mechanisms other than interfacial obstruction of dislocations may dominate creep behavior.
Oxidation or interfacial degradation during operation could reduce the effectiveness of the proposed interfacial-barrier mechanism.
A controlled series of thinner- and thicker-layer Al-Cr-Fe-Ni coatings can be compared under identical nanoindentation creep-loading conditions.

Failure of thinner-layer coatings to produce a statistically significant creep-rate reduction, or observation of inferior creep performance, would falsify the proposed governing role of increased interfacial density.
